claims.text: Replacing TOR-TILD's EAM reference with a Behler-Parrinello-type machine-learned potential trained on diverse ab initio liquid configurations will significantly improve reference-target phase-space overlap.
The machine-learned reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30-50% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The proposed method targets multicomponent high-entropy alloys in ordered solid and disordered liquid states near their melting temperatures.
The machine-learned potential should be trained on an extensive ab initio dataset containing both liquid and solid configurations for the compositions of interest.
The intervention is applicable to HEAs ranging from dilute substitutions to equiatomic compositions.
The intervention is applicable at temperatures just below or at the alloy melting point.
Atomic configurational diversity in HEA liquids is most pronounced near the melting point.
A machine-learned potential trained on diverse liquid structures can accurately capture a wide variety of liquid atomic arrangements.
Capturing a wider variety of liquid atomic arrangements improves reference-target phase-space overlap.
Training on ab initio data spanning diverse liquid configurations enables the potential to represent local atomic environments better than an EAM reference.
Better representation of local atomic environments minimizes mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
Reducing thermodynamic-integration path mismatch produces more precise free-energy calculations.
The machine-learned reference will yield melting free energies within a few meV/atom of full ab initio calculations.
TOR-TILD's EAM references provide poor phase-space overlap because they cannot capture the full diversity of liquid atomic configurations in HEAs.
The applicability of the intervention may diminish at lower temperatures.
The applicability of the intervention may diminish for systems whose configurational characteristics are absent from the training data.
Failure to reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by at least approximately 30% relative to the EAM baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
A melting free-energy deviation of more than a few meV/atom from full ab initio thermodynamic integration would falsify the hypothesis.
